# Capitalism versus Socialism

## Comparison between Capitalism and Socialism at the 10th Inter-University Seminar on Economics for Politics. Universidad de San Carlos de Guatemala, Guatemala, April 18, 2012. {.unnumbered}

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}
{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=05VO-FLrNi8 >}}
:::

The topic Professor Cristian proposed to me is comparative political and economic systems—that is, basically comparing capitalism and socialism. And following that, the question of which political form is best suited to foster one or the other. Among the various political forms existing today—the study of political forms has largely been neglected, yet forms remain deeply relevant: democracy, autocracy, dictatorship, monarchy—which is most suited to promote economic development? Which political form best nurtures these values? So this is an open debate to see what insights we can draw. Basically, I do not intend to deliver a very long lecture; I will lay out several key propositions and then we will discuss them.

Well, my thesis is singular and straightforward. First and foremost: socialism is evil and capitalism is good—free-market capitalism. It is that simple; if you take this away today, we will have learned plenty. Socialism is bad, write that down, and free-market capitalism is good; it is the only viable option. And you might ask: "Why?" In my modesty, I will point to four core features.

First: socialism is not free; socialism is totalitarian. "Why?" you might ask. Because without private property, there is no freedom. Without private property, freedom cannot exist. There can be no freedom of speech, no freedom of association, no freedom of movement, nor any other dimension of human liberty. Why this must be so is explained by a lineage of thinkers. I am thinking of the celebrated book *The Road to Serfdom* [@hayek1944road] by [Friedrich von Hayek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friedrich_Hayek)^[Austrian-born British economist, Nobel laureate in Economics.], a classic work that addresses this issue, demonstrating that any form of socialism—and when he speaks of socialism, he refers not only to Marxist socialism, but to social democracy, interventionism, and any framework that exerts institutional coercion over human beings, preventing them from trading or associating freely. We see this in Hayek's *The Road to Serfdom*, in [Wilhelm Röpke](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilhelm_R%C3%B6pke)^[German economist, one of the intellectual fathers of ordoliberalism.] in *The Social Crisis of Our Time* [@ropke1950social], in the works of [Mises](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ludwig_von_Mises)^[Austrian economist, leading figure of the Austrian School of Economics.], such as *Liberalism* [@vonmises1995liberalism], or in [Gottfried Dietze](https://mises.org/mises-daily/who-was-gottfried-dietze)^[Professor of Political Science at Johns Hopkins University.] in *In Defense of Property* [@dietze1963defense]. Dietze, a German scholar who emigrated to the United States, examines precisely this question.

Why can there be no freedom under socialism? Inwardly, in the privacy of our minds, we are all free. Within the sanctuary of our own thoughts, each of us is free; nobody can rule over our internal conscience. Each of us holds whatever thoughts we choose; there is no way to alter that by force. What *can* be prevented is our ability to express those thoughts and carry them into action. And to act upon them, to voice them publicly, we require freedom, and we require private property. That is to say: the expression of liberty always demands a material base.

To express freedom, we need communications media, we need paper, ink, printing presses, distribution logistics—in short, material capital goods. If we wish to convene an audience for a debate such as this one, we need an auditorium, a physical space, electricity, lighting, water, and so forth, to make that event possible. If we want to produce a television or radio show, we require a transmission station, a radio receiver, recording studios, cameras to film and broadcast, and if we want to use the internet, we need computers, network cables, server facilities, and physical spaces.

If the State owns all means of production, if the State monopolizes all wealth within a nation, where do you host a radio show? If you want to deliver an address like this one, where do you speak? You must ask permission. What did [Salvador Allende](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salvador_Allende)^[Chilean socialist politician, President of Chile from 1970 to 1973.] do in his day? Nothing extraordinary: did he impose formal censorship? No; he simply nationalized newsprint paper and nationalized replacement radio parts. There was no need to draft a censorship statute or a press gag law—he simply nationalized the paper supply and supplied paper exclusively to his supporters. Did he explicitly ban dissent? No, but he severed the material foundation of free expression. The same applies to any assembly, any association, any profession: if all productive assets belong to the State and I despise my job, where do I go? If every enterprise is state-owned, there is nowhere to go.

Thus, first and foremost, if everything is collective property under the State, freedom hinges entirely upon the arbitrary whim of the governing ruler. It is the ruler who dictates which books are published, which concerts may be performed, which lectures are permitted, and which religions may exist. First point: without private property, there is no freedom, because liberty invariably demands a physical base. Similarly in enterprise: if everything belongs to the State and I want to launch a business, buy an asset, or sell a product, I must obtain administrative permission, which may be granted or denied. Socialism cannot be free, because from the moment you must request permission to act, you are not free.

Second point: socialism is exploitative; capitalism is not. Socialism is inherently exploitative because it *must* be. When a socialist or Marxist critiques the market system, he does not criticize how wealth is spent. When [Bill Gates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Gates)^[American business magnate and philanthropist, co-founder of Microsoft.] dedicates vast portions of his fortune to charity, medical research, or poverty alleviation, he is not spared Marxist critique. They tell him: "No, the origin of your wealth lies in exploitation." How he subsequently spends it is deemed irrelevant. For the Marxist, the essence of the evil lies in how the capitalist acquired the wealth—allegedly by paying workers less than the value of their labor.

That premise is entirely false. Consider real-world socialist societies: Cuba, North Korea, the former Soviet Union, or Eastern Bloc nations. Did those societies lack armaments? Did they lack standing armies? Did they lack welfare systems and public infrastructure? Did they not pave roads and construct public facilities? How were those public goods financed under a socialist system? How was the Soviet military financed? How did they fund Sputnik? How did they build nuclear weapons? By paying workers less than the full value of their output! How else could an economic surplus be generated? For a socialist country to amass a surplus to sustain diplomacy, armies, and administrative bureaucracies, it must pay the laborer less than what his work produces. In those countries, by definition, there are no private taxes, since the State owns all assets; hence, public goods are financed directly at the expense of workers' wages.

Socialism necessarily underpays the worker by definition. Under free-market capitalism, where no coercive extraction exists, the worker receives the discounted marginal value of his labor. Under socialism, exploitation is forced upon one group by another. The [dacha](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dacha)^[Country house or second home in Russia.] of [Brezhnev](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonid_Brezhnev)^[Soviet politician who served as the General Secretary of the Communist Party.], the dachas of [Chernenko](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Konstantin_Chernenko)^[General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union.], the Black Sea palaces of Soviet elites, the [ZIL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZiL) luxury limousines reserved for party apparatchiks—at whose expense were they acquired? At the expense of shortchanging the worker through compulsory wage scales. Under socialism, labor is not free: if I dislike Guatemala City, I cannot move to Antigua without an internal passport and state permit. If I dislike my factory, I cannot switch employers; I am assigned to my workstation at a wage decreed by party bureaucrats. Any public luxury enjoyed by the political ruling class is extracted from the sweat of the working man. If one evaluates an economic system by how surplus is obtained rather than how it is spent, the socialist system is exploitative by definition. Furthermore, because wages are decreed politically rather than determined by supply and demand, certain favored groups receive more than their economic output warrants, financed by undercompensating everyone else.

Third, socialism is unjust; it is radically unjust by its very nature. Fundamentally, it fails to reward each individual according to what he contributes. If equal wages are enforced, the diligent worker earns the exact same as the loafer, unless capitalist incentive structures and wage differentials are reintroduced. Under socialism, rewards, promotions, and privileges are assigned politically, based on party loyalty or ideological alignment, rather than reflecting how much fellow citizens value one's contribution.

Nothing is more unjust than treating unequals equally. It is as if I assigned the exact same passing grade to all my university students regardless of effort: giving the same mark to the student who skips class and sleeps through lectures as to the student who arrives on time, works diligently, and completes every assignment. Would that be just? A system that rewards everyone identically is radically unjust at its core. Moreover, socialist mechanisms rely exclusively on political coercion: forcing individuals to obey decrees, restricting their movement, and subordinating their individual plans to a centralized supreme planning council. It denies individuals the freedom to pursue the career they desire, live where they choose, and think as they wish.

And fourth—most crucially of all—socialism cannot exist. It is not merely a question of whether it is morally good or bad: it is economically impossible, as the history of economic systems demonstrates. Why? Because socialism cannot calculate. I do not know if you are familiar with the socialist calculation debate. In the 1920s, a group of scholars—including the Russian economist [Boris Brutzkus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boris_Brutzkus), the German sociologist [Max Weber](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Max_Weber) in *Economy and Society* [@weber1921economy], Dutch Prime Minister [Nicolaas Pierson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaas_Pierson), and the Austrian economist Ludwig von Mises—formulated the question: is a socialist economic order possible? Not whether it is desirable, but whether it can physically function.

Their conclusion was decisive: even if administered by angels, a socialist order cannot function because without private property in capital goods, there are no markets; without markets, there are no prices; without prices, there is no economic calculation; and without economic calculation, complex production cannot be coordinated. Socialism collapses under its own blind irrationality.

Consider this: each of you carries between 8,000 and 15,000 words in your head. We use those words to communicate, formulate abstractions like "justice" or "beauty," and coordinate action. We don't reflect on this daily because since childhood we absorbed words incrementally. But what people overlook is that you also carry between 8,000 and 15,000 prices in your memory. From childhood, your parents taught you what was "expensive" or "cheap": the price of a pound of sugar, a gallon of fuel, a sweater, university tuition, or parking. You carry thousands of price benchmarks in your mind. Without those prices, you would be completely blind; you could not plan or calculate.

When choosing a university career, you weigh psychic satisfaction, but you also calculate future earnings against tuition costs. When traveling to Antigua, you can call a helicopter, hail a cab, drive a car, take a public bus, or ride a bicycle. If you are experiencing a medical emergency, you take an ambulance or charter a helicopter; if you want leisure, you stroll or cycle; for ordinary travel, you board a bus. How do you decide? By consulting prices in relation to your subjective urgency. If prices did not exist, why not summon a helicopter for every errand? Because you know a helicopter is tremendously expensive. You know that because market prices signal relative scarcity.

Imagine a world without prices, or where prices are fixed absurdly by decree, as in communist Poland where bread was subsidized to be cheaper than raw wheat. What did Polish farmers feed their pigs? Bread! Isn't feeding fresh baked bread to hogs a colossal misallocation of resources? Such absurdities were ubiquitous because prices were detached from market reality.

The only large-scale attempt at total abolition of markets and money was [War Communism](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_communism) in Soviet Russia (1918–1921), overseen theoretically by [Nikolai Bukharin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nikolai_Bukharin)^[Russian Bolshevik revolutionary and Marxist theorist.], an economist who had studied under [Böhm-Bawerk](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eugen_von_B%C3%B6hm-Bawerk) in Vienna and co-authored *The ABC of Communism* [@bukharin1920abc]. They nationalized all enterprises and attempted to abolish monetary transactions. The result was the steepest collapse in output recorded in modern history. As the Marxist economic historian [Alec Nove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Nove) documents in *An Economic History of the U.S.S.R.* [@nove1992economic], agricultural and industrial production plummeted to a minuscule fraction of pre-war levels within months. The disaster was so acute that [Lenin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vladimir_Lenin) and Bukharin were forced to retreat and introduce the [New Economic Policy (NEP)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Economic_Policy), restoring private trade and market mechanisms.

Marxists in this room might ask: "How did the Soviet Union survive for seven decades if calculation was impossible?" When Soviet planners under Gorbachev were asked how they established prices, they acknowledged: they consulted the Sears Roebuck catalog and the commodity price tables in the *Wall Street Journal*! They took prices formed in Western capitalist markets to resolve their internal input-output equations. Furthermore, they relied heavily on domestic black markets to gauge relative scarcities, and on historical memory. Ultimately, the Soviet system remained an intellectual parasite on the capitalist world. Indeed, some socialist theorists jokingly suggested that after the global communist revolution, New Zealand should be kept capitalist just to generate market prices for the rest of the planet!

What solution remains? Capitalism. Capitalism is just, because it is the only system founded on non-coercion—on voluntary agreement between contracting parties. The German sociologist [Franz Oppenheimer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franz_Oppenheimer)^[German-Jewish sociologist and political economist.], a social democrat himself, wrote a brilliant treatise, *The State* [@oppenheimer1908state], distinguishing two fundamentally opposed means of acquiring wealth: the economic means and the political means. The economic means is voluntary production and exchange, where both parties gain *ex ante*, otherwise they would not trade. The political means is the unrequited appropriation of the labor of others through coercion, taxation, and violence.

Capitalism operates exclusively through the economic means. It compensates each factor of production according to its discounted marginal productivity, as evaluated by consumers. People often dislike hearing this, but economically our market value is what other people are willing to pay for our services, not what our vanity believes we are worth.

Furthermore, capitalism is not exploitative. Even Marxist economic theory encounters an insurmountable contradiction here: if different industries possess different organic compositions of capital (ratios of machinery to labor), yet capital yields a uniform rate of profit across sectors, where does the uniform rate of profit come from if surplus value is extracted solely from living labor? [Eduard Bernstein](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eduard_Bernstein)^[Father of Marxist revisionism.] noted this unresolved riddle in Marx's framework. Profit does not stem from labor exploitation, but from the temporal discount and successful entrepreneurial foresight in coordinating resources.

Lastly, capitalism can calculate. Profit and loss serve as lighthouses in the dark: high profits signal to capital, "invest here, shift resources from where they satisfy fewer consumer desires toward where they satisfy more." Market prices communicate vast dispersed knowledge: what to produce, in what quantity, using which techniques, and in which locations. The alternative is surrender to a central dictator who arbitrarily dictates the livelihood of millions.

Which political systems favor capitalism? Capitalism is remarkably adaptable: it has flourished under monarchies, autocracies, republics, and even nominally communist regimes. Indeed, historical monarchies of the *Ancien Régime* were often well-suited to capitalism because their time preference was low and royal authority lacked democratic legitimacy, making subjects fiercely resistant to taxation. Today, former communist nations like China, Vietnam, and Eastern European states are implementing ambitious pro-market reforms—precisely because they experienced the nightmare of socialism firsthand and have no desire to return. What matters is not the constitutional label, but the institutional security of private property rights and economic liberty.

I will now open the floor to your questions.

### Question: "Under a capitalist system, how can extreme poverty be overcome?" {.unnumbered}

We tend to misunderstand poverty, as if global wealth were natural and poverty an anomaly. For thousands of years, the human condition was one of relentless, grinding poverty. Switzerland was poor, France was poor, England was poor. Across Europe until the nineteenth century, famine struck roughly every twenty years. If a crop failure occurred in Galicia, my homeland, while grain was plentiful in Germany, there was no physical infrastructure to transport food across the continent in time.

What began in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries in England, France, and America was capitalism: production aided by accumulated capital goods. What distinguishes a wealthy country from a poor country is capital endowment per capita. What distinguishes a Swiss farmer from a [Banyamulenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Banyamulenge) farmer in the mountains of the Congo? Why is Switzerland affluent while the Congo suffers? Because the Swiss farmer operates a 500-horsepower [Massey Ferguson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Massey_Ferguson) tractor; his physical labor is multiplied a thousandfold, producing in a single afternoon what required the toil of 200 laborers in the past. The African farmer works with bare hands or a wooden plow behind a frail ox; his productivity is a fraction of the capitalized worker's.

Wealthy nations became rich through frugality, high savings, and capital accumulation. Instead of carrying burdens on human backs, they constructed steam engines and rail networks. This multiplied marginal labor productivity, elevating wages. Poverty is the historical default; wealth is what requires explanation! Global life expectancy did not surpass 30 years until the advent of industrial capitalism in the twentieth century. Today, extreme poverty is lower than ever in recorded history.

Take Cuba in 1958: UN statistics show that pre-revolutionary Cuba had a per capita income on par with France and Austria, and double that of Italy and Spain. Today it languishes near the bottom of Latin America alongside Haiti and Honduras. Compare South Korea and Sudan in 1960: both possessed virtually identical per capita incomes. Sudan remained stagnant under interventionist governance; South Korea embraced market capitalism, multiplying its per capita income thirtyfold. That is the only real remedy for poverty: **capitalism, savings, and hard work!**

### Question: "Did socialism fail because past attempts were merely imperfect experiments? Did European colonialism exploit Latin America to finance European capitalism? What is the fair value of a worker?" {.unnumbered}

When debating economic systems, one must compare theory against theory, or real-world practice against real-world practice. Critics often compare real-world capitalism—burdened with regulations and crony state subsidies—against an idealized, utopian socialist fantasy. That is intellectually dishonest. Compare ideal capitalism with ideal socialism, or real-world socialist regimes with real-world capitalist economies. Theoretical socialism cannot function even if administered by saintly angels, because angels cannot overcome the absence of economic calculation.

Regarding colonialism: the thesis that Western nations grew rich by plundering colonies is historically inaccurate. Plunder has been ubiquitous throughout human history: Europeans were invaded by Moors, Huns, Mongols, and Vikings; Mesoamerican tribes subjugated neighboring peoples long before the Spanish arrived. Yet plunder does not create sustained industrial wealth. As Mises points out in *Nation, State, and Economy* [@vonmises1919nation], nations with no significant colonial empires—Switzerland, Norway, Sweden, Luxembourg, and Canada—are among the wealthiest on earth. Conversely, Portugal possessed one of the largest colonial empires relative to its size and remained Western Europe's poorest nation. As the Manchester School demonstrated, colonial empires were a political millstone around a nation's neck. British capital preferred investing in the United States, Argentina, and Brazil over its own colonies [@robbins1998history]. The gold and silver extracted by Spain simply sparked domestic price inflation and financed imperial dynastic wars; it did not foster sustainable industrial growth.

Regarding minimum wages and the value of labor: labor is an economic service, evaluated by consumers like any other. When you choose between taking a taxi or boarding a bus, you are actively pricing the driver's labor. A worker's wage reflects what consumers are willing to pay for his marginal output. In Galicia, my late grandfather worked from age nine in agriculture and canning; he worked seven days a week because cattle must be tended every single day. Yet through hard work, frugal saving, and capital accumulation, he laid the financial foundation that allowed my father and me to pursue higher education. Progress takes time—it requires generations of capital accumulation, not legislative decree.

### Question: "What are the negative effects of the capitalist system?" {.unnumbered}

It has none inherent to its nature, because capitalism consists entirely of voluntary agreements between consenting parties. If two individuals voluntarily agree to an exchange, it is because both perceive a mutual benefit. Where interaction is strictly peaceful and voluntary, no systemic injury can occur.

### Question: "Why hasn't Guatemala prospered if it is a capitalist country?" {.unnumbered}

Look up the [Heritage Index of Economic Freedom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Index_of_Economic_Freedom) and see where Guatemala ranks. Economic freedom measures the rule of law, property rights security, bureaucratic ease of launching a business, and regulatory burdens. Guatemala's economy is heavily intervened, laden with bureaucratic red tape and crony protections. It is far from an unhampered free market.

### Question: "How can development be achieved when 85% of land is concentrated in 5% of hands?" {.unnumbered}

Consider this: why does an imported automobile cost nearly 60% more here in Guatemala than in Spain, a country with higher average wages? Why do imported consumer goods carry a 50% to 60% markup? Because of brutal import tariffs and state protectionism! That is not capitalism; that is mercantilism that impoverishes Guatemalan consumers and protects entrenched monopolies. Remove tariffs, eliminate privileges, protect property rights, and prosperity will follow.
